title: Practice Lab 1: NASA Open APIs
text:
NASA provides free, production-quality APIs used by researchers worldwide. In this lab you will work with two:

APOD — Astronomy Picture of the Day: one endpoint, one JSON object, a clean introduction.
NEO — Near-Earth Object Web Service: asteroid data with a deeply nested response structure that requires real parsing work.

Auth pattern: API key as a URL query parameter (?api_key=YOUR_KEY).

text:
Step 1 — Get Your API Key

Go to api.nasa.gov
Fill in the short registration form and submit
Your key arrives by email within minutes
Add it to your .Renviron file:

NASA_KEY=your_key_here






NoteDEMO_KEY — No signup needed



NASA provides a built-in demo key. Replace nasa_key with "DEMO_KEY" anywhere in this lab. It allows 30 requests/hour and 50/day — enough to complete the exercises.

section: Exercise 1: Astronomy Picture of the Day
text:
Exercise 1: Astronomy Picture of the Day
The APOD endpoint returns a single JSON object describing today’s featured image or video, along with a scientific explanation written by a professional astronomer.

apod_url <- glue("https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod?api_key={nasa_key}")

req      <- request(apod_url)
response <- req_perform(req)

# Always check the status first
resp_status(response)


apod <- resp_body_json(response)

# Inspect the top-level keys
names(apod)


cat("Title:     ", apod$title,      "\n")
cat("Date:      ", apod$date,       "\n")
cat("Media type:", apod$media_type, "\n")
cat("URL:       ", apod$url,        "\n")
cat("\nExplanation:\n", apod$explanation, "\n")


Challenge A — Request a Specific Date
Add a date query parameter to retrieve any past APOD. Dates go back to 1995-06-16.

apod_dated_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
  "?api_key={nasa_key}&date=1995-06-16"
)

apod_first <- resp_body_json(req_perform(request(apod_dated_url)))
cat("First ever APOD:", apod_first$title, "\n")



Challenge B — Retrieve a Batch of APODs
Use the count parameter to retrieve multiple random APODs in a single request.

apod_batch_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod",
  "?api_key={nasa_key}&count=5"
)

apod_list <- resp_body_json(req_perform(request(apod_batch_url)))

# How is the structure different from a single APOD?
length(apod_list)
apod_list[[1]]$title

title: Practice Lab 1: NASA Open APIs
text:
Exercise 2: Near-Earth Object (Asteroid) Data
The NEO endpoint returns every asteroid that passed near Earth within a date range. The response is nested three levels deep — a great exercise in list navigation.

neo_url <- glue(
  "https://api.nasa.gov/neo/rest/v1/feed",
  "?start_date=2024-01-01&end_date=2024-01-07",
  "&api_key={nasa_key}"
)

response <- req_perform(request(neo_url))
neo_data <- resp_body_json(response)

cat("Total asteroids in this range:", neo_data$element_count, "\n")
cat("Top-level keys:", paste(names(neo_data), collapse=", "), "\n")


# Near-Earth objects are nested: neo_data$near_earth_objects → date → list of asteroids
dates <- names(neo_data$near_earth_objects)
cat("Dates in response:", paste(dates, collapse=", "), "\n")

# Look at the first asteroid on the first date
first_day   <- neo_data$near_earth_objects[[dates[1]]]
first_rock  <- first_day[[1]]

cat("Name:", first_rock$name, "\n")
cat("Hazardous?", first_rock$is_potentially_hazardous_asteroid, "\n")
cat("Min diameter (km):",
    first_rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_min, "\n")


# Flatten all dates and asteroids into a single data frame
all_asteroids <- lapply(neo_data$near_earth_objects, function(day) {
  lapply(day, function(rock) {
    data.frame(
      name          = rock$name,
      date          = rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$close_approach_date,
      is_hazardous  = rock$is_potentially_hazardous_asteroid,
      min_diam_km   = rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_min,
      max_diam_km   = rock$estimated_diameter$kilometers$estimated_diameter_max,
      miss_dist_km  = as.numeric(rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$miss_distance$kilometers),
      speed_kmh     = as.numeric(rock$close_approach_data[[1]]$relative_velocity$kilometers_per_hour)
    )
  }) |> bind_rows()
}) |> bind_rows()

glimpse(all_asteroids)


ggplot(all_asteroids, aes(x = miss_dist_km / 1e6, fill = is_hazardous)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, alpha = 0.85, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#4f46e5", "TRUE" = "#ef4444"),
    labels = c("Not Hazardous", "Potentially Hazardous")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Asteroid Miss Distances — Jan 1–7, 2024",
    subtitle = "Each bar = one asteroid; distance from Earth's center",
    x        = "Miss Distance (millions of km)",
    y        = "Count",
    fill     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Practice Lab 1: NASA Open APIs
text:
Questions

———————


Q1.
(Conceptual): In this lab the API key is passed as a query parameter (?api_key=...). Name one situation where this approach could create a security risk.






TipAnswer Q1





The key is visible in the URL — which means it appears in browser history, server access logs, and anywhere the URL is copy-pasted or shared. If you accidentally post the URL in a public place (a GitHub issue, a Slack message, a screenshot), your key is exposed. Header-based auth keeps the credential out of the URL entirely.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Code): The count parameter returns a list of APODs instead of a single object. Write code that extracts just the title from each item in the batch and prints them as a character vector.






TipAnswer Q2





titles <- sapply(apod_list, function(x) x$title)
print(titles)
sapply maps a function over each list element and simplifies the result to a vector.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Analysis): After building all_asteroids, use dplyr to find the single asteroid with the smallest miss distance in the date range. Was it potentially hazardous?






TipAnswer Q3





all_asteroids |>
  arrange(miss_dist_km) |>
  select(name, date, miss_dist_km, is_hazardous) |>
  slice(1)
The answer varies by date range, but notice whether is_hazardous is TRUE for the closest pass — this is the heart of what NASA tracks with NEO Watch.




———————

title: Practice Lab 5: GitHub REST API
text:
The GitHub REST API is the most realistic example in this workshop — it is a production API used by millions of developers daily. It introduces two concepts you haven’t seen yet:

No-auth public access — many endpoints work without any credential, though with strict rate limits
Fine-grained Personal Access Tokens (PATs) — scoped tokens where you explicitly choose what permissions to grant

The PAT exercise is a live demonstration of least-privilege security: only give a credential exactly the access it needs, and nothing more.
Auth patterns: None (public) → Bearer token with Authorization: Bearer TOKEN.

Exercise 1: Retrieve Public Repository Data (No Auth)

# GitHub requires a User-Agent header — always include it
req <- request("https://api.github.com/users/hadley/repos") |>
  req_headers(
    Accept       = "application/vnd.github+json",
    `User-Agent` = "API-Workshop-Student"
  ) |>
  req_url_query(per_page = 30, sort = "updated")

response <- req_perform(req)

cat("Status:", resp_status(response), "\n")
cat("Rate limit remaining:", resp_header(response, "x-ratelimit-remaining"), "\n")


repos <- resp_body_json(response)

repos_df <- lapply(repos, function(r) {
  data.frame(
    name            = r$name,
    description     = substr(r$description %||% "", 1, 80),
    language        = r$language %||% NA_character_,
    stars           = r$stargazers_count,
    forks           = r$forks_count,
    open_issues     = r$open_issues_count,
    is_fork         = r$fork,
    created_at      = r$created_at,
    updated_at      = r$updated_at
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

repos_df |>
  arrange(desc(stars)) |>
  select(name, language, stars, forks) |>
  head(10)







NoteRate Limits Without Auth



Unauthenticated requests are limited to 60 per hour (shared by your IP address). The x-ratelimit-remaining header tells you how many you have left. With a PAT, the limit rises to 5,000 per hour.

title: Practice Lab 5: GitHub REST API
section: Exercise 3: Create a Fine-Grained Personal Access Token
text:
Exercise 3: Create a Fine-Grained Personal Access Token

Step 3a — Create the Token

Go to github.com → your avatar → Settings
Scroll to Developer Settings → Personal Access Tokens → Fine-grained tokens
Click Generate new token
Set:

Token name: api-workshop-lab
Expiration: 7 days
Resource owner: your account
Repository access: Public repositories only
Permissions: Metadata → Read-only (this is the minimum needed)

Click Generate token and copy it immediately — it won’t be shown again
Add it to your .Renviron:

GITHUB_TOKEN=your_token_here






ImportantWhat You Just Did



You created a token with the minimum necessary permissions: read access to metadata on public repositories only. Even if this token leaked, an attacker could only read public data — they could not write code, delete repositories, or access private data. This is the principle of least privilege.




Step 3b — Use the Token

load_dot_env()
github_token <- Sys.getenv("GITHUB_TOKEN")


# Authenticated request — now you get 5000 requests/hour
req <- request("https://api.github.com/user") |>
  req_headers(
    Authorization = glue("Bearer {github_token}"),
    Accept        = "application/vnd.github+json",
    `User-Agent`  = "API-Workshop-Student"
  )

response  <- req_perform(req)
user_data <- resp_body_json(response)

cat("Authenticated as:", user_data$login, "\n")
cat("Rate limit remaining:", resp_header(response, "x-ratelimit-remaining"), "\n")

title: Practice Lab 5: GitHub REST API
text:
Questions

———————


Q1.
(Conceptual): In Exercise 1, you saw the x-ratelimit-remaining header in the response. Why would an API designer include rate limit information in the response headers rather than (or in addition to) the response body?






TipAnswer Q1





Headers deliver metadata about the response — information about the exchange itself, not the data you requested. Putting rate limit info in headers keeps the response body clean and focused on the requested data. It also means client code can check rate limits without parsing the body — a faster, more efficient check. This is the standard HTTP convention: data goes in the body, metadata goes in headers.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Security): You created a fine-grained token with read-only access to public repositories. Describe a scenario where even this minimal token could be misused if it leaked publicly.






TipAnswer Q2





An attacker with a public-read token could: - Scrape your public repository data at the 5,000 req/hour authenticated rate (vs. 60/hour unauthenticated) — useful for mass enumeration - Identify which public repos you contribute to, revealing professional affiliations or project work you hadn’t publicized - Burn through your rate limit, causing your own API calls to fail
This is why even minimal tokens should be rotated (deleted and regenerated) quickly if leaked, and why expiry dates are important — a 7-day token automatically becomes useless.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Extension): Modify the repository search from Exercise 2 to collect all pages of results (not just the first 20). GitHub limits search results to 1,000 total — use total_count and per_page to calculate how many pages to fetch, and use Sys.sleep(1) between requests to avoid hitting rate limits.






TipAnswer Q3





search_all_github <- function(query, token, max_results = 100) {
  per_page   <- 30
  total_pages <- ceiling(min(max_results, 1000) / per_page)

  all_results <- lapply(seq_len(total_pages), function(p) {
    Sys.sleep(1)  # be a polite client
    req <- request("https://api.github.com/search/repositories") |>
      req_headers(
        Authorization = glue("Bearer {token}"),
        Accept        = "application/vnd.github+json",
        `User-Agent`  = "API-Workshop-Student"
      ) |>
      req_url_query(q = query, sort = "stars", per_page = per_page, page = p)

    data <- resp_body_json(req_perform(req))
    lapply(data$items, function(r) {
      data.frame(name = r$full_name, stars = r$stargazers_count, language = r$language %||% NA)
    }) |> bind_rows()
  }) |> bind_rows()

  all_results
}
Sys.sleep(1) adds a 1-second pause between pages. This is good API citizenship — it avoids triggering abuse detection and spreads requests over time.




———————

text:
Part 1: Extract — Historical Weather Data
Open-Meteo has a second endpoint for past weather — the archive endpoint:
https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive
Browser first, as always. Paste this — it asks for San Luis Obispo’s daily high and low temperatures for one week in July 2025:
https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&start_date=2025-07-01&end_date=2025-07-07&daily=temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&timezone=auto
Two new query parameters do the date work: start_date and end_date. And here’s the good news — one request returns the entire date range. No loops needed.
Now in R:

# E: extract -------------------------------------------------
result <- request("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = 35.28,
    longitude = -120.66,
    start_date = "2025-07-01",
    end_date = "2025-07-07",
    daily = "temperature_2m_max,temperature_2m_min",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit",
    timezone = "auto"
  ) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

# Peek at the daily piece
str(result$daily, max.level = 1)

The daily element is a named list of three parallel lists: time, temperature_2m_max, and temperature_2m_min — one entry per day.

# T: transform ------------------------------------------------
slo_df <- tibble(
  city     = "San Luis Obispo",
  date     = as.Date(unlist(result$daily$time)),
  temp_max = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_max),
  temp_min = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_min)
)

slo_df







NoteWhy unlist()?



resp_body_json() parses each JSON array into an R list. unlist() flattens that list into a plain vector, which is what a tibble column needs. List in, vector out — that’s all it does.



———————


Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): To ask the archive endpoint for a different range of days, we change the ________ and ________ query parameters.






TipAnswer Q1





start_date and end_date. Everything else in the request can stay exactly the same.

———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): What does unlist() do in the Transform step?

It flattens a list into a plain vector so it can be a tibble column.
It sends the request to the server.
It removes missing values from the data.
It converts Fahrenheit to Celsius.
It sorts the dates in order.







TipAnswer Q2





a) JSON arrays arrive in R as lists; unlist() turns each one into a vector — exactly what tibble columns are made of.

Part 3: Boston vs. San Luis Obispo — Two Simple Comparisons
Let’s use the map() pattern from Session 3 to compare two cities. The recipe below fetches one city’s daily highs for any date range:

cities <- tribble(
  ~city,             ~latitude, ~longitude,
  "San Luis Obispo",     35.28,    -120.66,
  "Boston",              42.36,     -71.06
)


Comparison 1: Summer

# E + T for both cities: July 2025
summer_df <- cities |>
  pmap(\(city, latitude, longitude) {

    result <- request("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive") |>
      req_url_query(
        latitude = latitude,
        longitude = longitude,
        start_date = "2025-07-01",
        end_date = "2025-07-31",
        daily = "temperature_2m_max",
        temperature_unit = "fahrenheit",
        timezone = "auto"
      ) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    tibble(
      city     = city,
      date     = as.Date(unlist(result$daily$time)),
      temp_max = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_max)
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

# V: one line per city
ggplot(summer_df, aes(x = date, y = temp_max, color = city)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Summer Daily Highs: Boston vs. San Luis Obispo",
    subtitle = "July 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily High (°F)",
    color = "City"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)


———————



Q4 — Visual Check (Summer).
(Multiple Choice): In the summer plot, what distinguishes Boston’s line from San Luis Obispo’s line?

The line type (solid vs. dashed)
The x-axis position
Separate panels for each city
The point shape
The line color, mapped with aes(color = city)







TipAnswer Q4





e) We mapped the city column to the color aesthetic — aes(color = city) — so ggplot automatically draws one colored line per city and builds the legend.




———————



Comparison 2: Winter
Same recipe — the only change is the two dates:

# E + T for both cities: January 2026
winter_df <- cities |>
  pmap(\(city, latitude, longitude) {

    result <- request("https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive") |>
      req_url_query(
        latitude = latitude,
        longitude = longitude,
        start_date = "2026-01-01",
        end_date = "2026-01-31",
        daily = "temperature_2m_max",
        temperature_unit = "fahrenheit",
        timezone = "auto"
      ) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    tibble(
      city     = city,
      date     = as.Date(unlist(result$daily$time)),
      temp_max = unlist(result$daily$temperature_2m_max)
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

# V
ggplot(winter_df, aes(x = date, y = temp_max, color = city)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Winter Daily Highs: Boston vs. San Luis Obispo",
    subtitle = "January 2026",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily High (°F)",
    color = "City"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)


———————



Q5 — Visual Check (Winter).
(Multiple Choice): Comparing the summer and winter code blocks, what changed between them?

The endpoint changed to a winter-specific API.
An API key was added for winter data.
Only the start_date and end_date values changed.
The cities table had to be rebuilt.
pmap() was replaced by a for loop.







TipAnswer Q5





c) Two date strings — that’s the entire difference. Same endpoint, same recipe, same transform, same plot code. This is the power of the ETV pattern: new question, two small edits.




———————


———————



Q6.
(Fill in the Blank): In both comparison plots, we expect ________ to show much colder daily highs in January, while San Luis Obispo stays mild year-round.






TipAnswer Q6





Boston. Coastal California has a mild Mediterranean climate; Boston winters regularly stay below freezing — the winter plot makes the gap dramatic, often 30–40°F.

text:
Part 5: Reflection & Pitfalls

Common Pitfalls When Working with APIs

Rate Limits: Most APIs limit how many requests you can make per minute/hour (Open-Meteo’s free tier allows ~10,000 calls/day — generous, but not infinite). Design your code to respect limits.
API Keys (elsewhere): Most commercial APIs require keys. When you use one, never write the key directly in your script — store it in an environment file. The Practice Labs on this site walk through this.
Data Structure Changes: API providers can change their response format without warning. Always inspect the structure of new responses (str()) before building pipelines around them.
URL Encoding: Special characters (spaces, ampersands, accents) must be encoded in URLs. req_url_query() handles this for you automatically — one more reason to like it.
Nested JSON Complexity: Real-world JSON can be deeply nested. Practice with str() and names() to navigate the structure before trying to flatten it.



Reflection Questions for Your Practice

Where could API data naturally integrate into your curriculum?
What are the pitfalls (rate limits, authentication) that students need to know?
How does working with live, messy data differ from working with pre-cleaned datasets?
What ethical considerations arise when collecting data from APIs?

title: Session 2: CRUD, HTTP Methods & URL Anatomy
text:
Part 1: The CRUD Framework
What type of client requests can we make? The CRUD framework organizes the four fundamental operations.

Look First



Now in Words
The image maps each CRUD operation to a visual icon: a plus sign for Create/POST (adding something new), an eye for Read/GET (looking at existing data), a pencil for Update/PUT-PATCH (editing something), and a trash can for Delete/DELETE (removing it).



CRUD Operation
HTTP Method
Description




Create
POST
Submit new data to the server


Read
GET
Retrieve existing data from the server


Update
PUT / PATCH
Modify existing data on the server


Delete
DELETE
Remove a resource from the server









NoteFor Data Science



In data science, Read (GET) is by far the most common operation. We’re typically pulling data, not writing to databases. As a data scientist, the eye (Read/GET) quadrant will cover the vast majority of your API work.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



Our workshop goal — make a request, format the response — lives almost entirely in the Read (GET) quadrant. Everything we do tomorrow is a GET.



———————



Visual Check — CRUD Operations.
(Multiple Choice): A social media app lets users edit their display name. Based on the image above, which CRUD operation and HTTP method does that action map to?

Create — POST
Read — GET
Delete — DELETE
Update — PUT/PATCH
Read — POST







TipAnswer — Visual Check





d) Update — PUT/PATCH. Editing an existing record (changing a name that already exists) is an Update operation — the pencil icon. It is not Create (nothing new is being added) or Read (data is being changed, not just viewed).




———————


———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): The HTTP method used to read (retrieve) data from a server is ________.






TipAnswer Q1





GET. Read = GET, and it is by far the most common operation in data science API work.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): Which CRUD operation is most commonly used in data science when working with APIs?

Read
Create
Update
Delete
All four equally







TipAnswer Q2





a) Read. Data scientists most commonly use GET requests to read (retrieve) data from external sources. We’re consumers of data, not typically writing to external databases.




———————

title: Session 2: CRUD, HTTP Methods & URL Anatomy
text:
Part 2: GET Requests
A GET request is all about retrieving data. You’re asking the server: “Give me this information.”

Watch First
Step through the GET request at your own pace — Next, Back, or press Play.



Now in Words
The animation shows a GET request for the resource GET /users/42. The request originates at the Client and travels through the API to the Server and Database. Notice two things: first, the request carries only a path (/users/42) — no data payload. Second, the response brings data back to the client while nothing new is written to the database.
Here is the flow of a GET request:

Client constructs a request for a resource.
API receives and validates the client’s request.
Server locates the requested data within the database.
Client receives the requested data from the server.







NoteGET Characteristics




The request parameters are encoded in the URL (visible in the address bar)
GET requests are meant to be read-only — they don’t change data on the server
They are idempotent — making the same request multiple times gives the same result









Tip🎯 Goal Check



“Make a request” in our goal sentence means, concretely: send a GET request — a URL asking for data.



———————



Visual Check — GET Request.
(Fill in the Blank): The animation shows GET /users/42. If you changed the request to GET /users/7, the only thing that changes is the ________ — the method, the flow, and everything else stay the same.






TipAnswer — Visual Check





The path (specifically, the number identifying which user you want — 42 becomes 7). The HTTP method is still GET and the flow (client → API → server → database → back) is identical.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Multiple Choice): Which of the following is an example of a task a data scientist would do with a GET request?

Deleting old records from a company database
Uploading a new profile photo
Posting a comment on a forum
Changing your account password
Retrieving the top 10 most popular articles from the New York Times API







TipAnswer Q3





e) Retrieving articles is reading existing data — a GET. The other four options all change something on the server (delete, create, create, update).




———————

title: Session 2: CRUD, HTTP Methods & URL Anatomy
text:
Part 3: POST Requests
A POST request is about sending new data to the server. You’re telling the server: “Here’s something new — store it.”

Watch First
Step through the POST request — watch where the payload starts and where it ends up.



Now in Words
The animation shows a POST request sending POST /users with a JSON payload { "name": "Maya", "email": "maya@example.com" }. Compare this carefully to the GET animation: with GET, data flowed from the server to the client. With POST, data originates at the client and moves toward the server. The client is the source; the server is the destination.
Here is the flow of a POST request:

Client sends new data within the request body.
API receives and validates the client’s new data.
Server creates a new record in the database.
Client receives a confirmation for the new record.







ImportantGET vs. POST — Key Difference




GET sends parameters in the URL — you’re asking for data.
POST sends data in the request body — you’re submitting new data.

Think of it this way: GET is reading a book from the library. POST is donating a new book to the library.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



POST is good to recognize, but our goal only needs GET. If POST feels fuzzy, that’s fine — it will not block anything we do tomorrow.



———————



Visual Check — POST Request.
(Multiple Choice): In the POST animation, the JSON payload { "name": "Maya", ... } travels from the Client to the Server. Where does this data live in the request?

In the URL query string, just like GET parameters.
In the request body — unlike GET, which puts parameters in the URL.
In a separate file attachment.
In the status code.
In the database before the request is even sent.







TipAnswer — Visual Check





b) POST sends data in the request body — a separate payload attached to the request. GET requests have no body; all their parameters are encoded directly in the URL (visible in the address bar).




———————


———————



Q4.
(Multiple Choice): Which of the following data science tasks would most likely require a POST request instead of a GET request?

Retrieving the current temperature for a city.
Getting a list of your public repositories from the GitHub API.
Submitting a new tweet through the X (formerly Twitter) API.
Looking up the coordinates for a specific address.
Downloading yesterday’s stock prices.







TipAnswer Q4





c) Submitting a new tweet involves creating a new resource on the server, which is the primary purpose of a POST request. The other options involve only retrieving existing data.




———————


———————



Q5.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to the restaurant analogy): If a GET request is like reading the menu and placing an order, what would a POST request be most analogous to?

Submitting a new recipe for the kitchen to keep in its collection
Asking the waiter to repeat the specials
Paying the bill with exact change
Ordering the same dish twice
Reading the menu a second time







TipAnswer Q5





a) A POST adds something new to the restaurant’s collection — like submitting a new recipe. Options b, d, and e are all just reading/asking again (GET-like), and paying the bill doesn’t add new data to the kitchen.




———————

title: Session 2: CRUD, HTTP Methods & URL Anatomy
text:
Part 4: URL Anatomy
So how do we actually construct a request? A request is defined by a URL, which contains both:

The endpoint (base address of the API) — the stable part
The query string (key-value pairs that customize the request) — the dynamic part


Watch First
Step through the URL piece by piece — each click highlights the next component.



Now in Words
The animation shows the Client (left) and API Server (right) with the URL being broken down between them. The full URL carries everything the server needs — protocol, host, endpoint path, and each query parameter — in a single string. Pay attention to where the endpoint ends and where the query string begins.


Breaking Down a URL
Here is a real URL we will use tomorrow — it asks the free Open-Meteo weather API for the current temperature in San Luis Obispo:
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit



Component
Value
Purpose




Protocol
https://
Secure communication


Base URL
api.open-meteo.com
The API server


Endpoint
/v1/forecast
Which resource you want


Query separator
?
Marks the start of parameters


Parameter 1
latitude=35.28
Where (north–south)


Parameter separator
&
Separates key-value pairs


Parameter 2
longitude=-120.66
Where (east–west)


Parameter 3
current=temperature_2m
What data you want


Parameter 4
temperature_unit=fahrenheit
Unit preference









NoteKey Vocabulary




An endpoint is the specific URL where an API resource can be accessed. It’s the stable part of the URL that doesn’t change from one request to the next.
A query string customizes the request using key-value pairs. It always starts with ? and pairs are separated by &.









NoteWhat About API Keys?



Many APIs require one extra query parameter: an API key (e.g., &appid=YOUR_KEY) — an ID that says who is making the request. The Open-Meteo API we use in this workshop is free and does not need a key, so our URLs stay short and simple. Just know the concept exists — you’ll see it in other APIs’ documentation.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



This is the “make a request” half of our goal, fully unpacked: a request = endpoint + query string. Tomorrow we paste this exact URL into a browser and into R.



———————



Visual Check — URL Anatomy.
(Fill in the Blanks): One character each.

The character that marks the boundary between the endpoint and the query string is ____.
The character that separates one key-value pair from the next is ____.







TipAnswer — Visual Check






The ? — everything before it is the stable address; everything after it is customization.
The & — it chains multiple key-value pairs together.





———————


———————



Q6.
(Short Answer): In the URL https://api.spotify.com/v1/search?q=Daft+Punk&type=artist, identify the endpoint and the two key-value pairs that make up the query string.






TipAnswer Q6






Endpoint: https://api.spotify.com/v1/search
Key-Value Pairs: q=Daft+Punk and type=artist





———————


———————



Q7.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Session 1): When your R script makes a GET request to a weather API, which statement is correct?

Your script sends JSON and receives a URL.
Your script sends JSON and receives JSON.
Your script sends a URL and receives a URL.
Your script sends a URL and receives JSON.
Your script sends a data frame and receives a plot.







TipAnswer Q7





d) The request itself is a carefully constructed URL containing the endpoint and query parameters. The API’s response comes back as JSON containing the data, metadata, and status code.




———————

Optional — After the Workshop: Going Deeper






WarningRead This Later, Not Today



The three sections below are optional enrichment — we will not cover them live. They preview the R code you’ll see in Sessions 3–4 and go deeper into error handling. If today already felt like a lot, skip this entirely; nothing tomorrow depends on it.



Optional A: Under the Hood — What Happens When You Make a Request
Let’s connect everything together:

You construct a URL from a base URL (endpoint) + query string (parameters).
Your client sends a GET request using this URL to the API.
The API relays this request to the server.
The server processes the request, queries the database, and sends a response.
The response includes a status code and the requested data (formatted as JSON).
Your R code parses the JSON into a data structure you can work with.







ImportantCommon Misconception



We are not sending JSON when we make a GET request. We’re sending a URL with parameters. JSON is what comes back to us in the response.




Optional B: Making Requests to a Dummy Server in R
These blocks show real requests to a practice server. You can run them any time after the workshop.

library(httr2)       # Makes web requests
library(tibble)      # Tidyverse data frames
library(dplyr)       # Data manipulation
library(glue)        # String construction

A simple GET request to a public test API:

# Step 1: Define the URL
test_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1"

# Step 2: Create a request object
req <- request(test_url)

# Step 3: Perform the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code
resp_status(response)

# Step 5: Check the content type
resp_content_type(response)


# Step 6: Parse the JSON response
result <- resp_body_json(response)

# Step 7: Inspect the structure
str(result)


# Step 8: Convert to a data frame
user_df <- as.data.frame(result)
print(user_df)

A GET request with query parameters:

# Get posts by a specific user
posts_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts"

posts_url_query <- glue("{posts_url}?userId=1")

req <- request(posts_url_query)
response <- req_perform(req)

if (resp_status(response) == 200) {
  posts <- resp_body_json(response)
  cat("Number of posts retrieved:", length(posts), "\n")
}

And a POST request — sending data to the server:

# Step 1: Define the endpoint
post_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts"

# Step 2: Create the request with a body
req <- request(post_url) |>
  req_method("POST") |>
  req_headers("Content-Type" = "application/json") |>
  req_body_json(list(
    title = "My API Workshop Post",
    body = "Learning about APIs is fun!",
    userId = 1
  ))

# Step 3: Perform the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code (201 = Created)
cat("Status:", resp_status(response), "\n")

# Step 5: See the response
result <- resp_body_json(response)
print(result)







NoteStatus Code 201



Notice we got a 201 Created instead of 200 OK. This is the standard success code for POST requests — it means the server successfully created the new resource.




Optional C: Handling Errors with Status Codes

# Try requesting a resource that doesn't exist
bad_url <- "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/999999"

req <- request(bad_url)
response <- req_perform(req)

# Check the status
cat("Status code:", resp_status(response), "\n")


# Build a robust request handler
safe_get <- function(url) {
  req <- request(url)
  response <- req_perform(req)
  status <- resp_status(response)

  if (status == 200) {
    cat("Success! Status:", status, "\n")
    return(resp_body_json(response))
  } else if (status >= 400 & status < 500) {
    cat("Client error! Status:", status, "- Check your URL or parameters.\n")
    return(NULL)
  } else if (status >= 500) {
    cat("Server error! Status:", status, "- The server has an issue.\n")
    return(NULL)
  }
}

# Test it
result <- safe_get("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1")


———————



Bonus Q.
(Open-Ended): In the GET request to the dummy server, we sent a URL and received JSON. In the POST request, we sent JSON in the request body. How does this change what we learned about GET vs. POST?






TipAnswer — Bonus Q





This reinforces the key difference: GET requests encode parameters in the URL and receive JSON back. POST requests send data in the request body (often as JSON) and receive a confirmation (also JSON) back. So POST actually involves JSON going both directions, while GET only involves JSON coming back.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
text:
Part 1: What is an API?
API stands for Application Programming Interface. At its core, an API is a way for software to communicate with other software. In data science, we use APIs to programmatically request data from external servers — weather services, sports databases, social media platforms, and more.

Watch First: The Restaurant Analogy
Use the buttons to step through the animation — go at your own pace, pause, or replay any step.

  
    
      🙋Youthe Client
    
    ⇄
    
      🤵Waiterthe API
    
    ⇄
    
      👨‍🍳Kitchenthe Server
    
    ⇄
    
      🧊Fridgethe Database
    
  
  
  
    ⏮ Restart
    ◀ Back
    
    Next ▶
    ▶ Play
  





Now in Words
Here is the same story, written out:

You (the client) look at the menu and make a request — you place your order.
The waiter (the API) carries your request to the kitchen.
The kitchen (the server, with its fridge — the database) prepares your food.
The waiter brings back your meal (the response).

The key insight: you never walk into the kitchen yourself. The API is the controlled interface that lets you interact with the data source. And notice who starts everything: the client makes the request. Nothing happens until you order.






Tip🎯 Goal Check



In this analogy, our workshop goal is simply: place an order (make a request) and turn the meal that arrives (the response) into something we can analyze.



———————



Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): In the restaurant analogy, the waiter plays the role of the ________.






TipAnswer Q1





The API. The waiter is the go-between: it carries your request to the kitchen (server) and brings the response back to you (client).




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): What is the primary utility of a web API for a data analyst?

To create visual websites for data projects.
To store large CSV files in the cloud.
To design the database structure for a server.
To allow programmatic, repeatable, and direct access to live data from an external source.
To replace the need for any programming language.







TipAnswer Q2





d) An API provides a structured way for a program (like an R script) to directly request and receive live data, making data acquisition automated and scalable.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
text:
Part 2: API Data Flow
Let’s go deeper into the architecture — same story as the restaurant, now with the technical names.

Watch First
Step through the request and response at your own pace — Next, Back, or press Play.



Now in Words
The animation traces a single API call from start to finish. There are four components in the chain: the Client (your R script or browser), the API (the endpoint — the “front door”), the Server (backend logic that processes the request), and the Database (where the actual data lives).
Request direction: Client (request) → API → Server → Database
Response direction: Client ← API ← Server (response) ← Database
The request moves left to right; the response travels the same path in reverse.






NoteKey Observations




The client is your R script or browser — anything making the request.
The API is the endpoint — the “front door” of the data service.
The server processes the request and queries the database.
The response travels back the same path.
A client and server can exist on the same computer — this is common in local development.









Tip🎯 Goal Check



This chain is exactly what happens every time we run our workshop goal: the client (our R script) makes a request, and a response comes back for us to analyze.



———————



Visual Check — API Data Flow.
(Multiple Choice): In the animation, the API sits between the Client and the Server. What best describes the API’s role in this chain?

It stores the data permanently.
It runs the backend logic that queries the database.
It acts as a gateway — receiving requests from the client and routing them to the server.
It is the same as the database.
It draws the plots at the end of the analysis.







TipAnswer — Visual Check





c) The API is a gateway or controlled interface. It does not store data (that’s the database) and it does not run the core business logic (that’s the server). It is the stable “front door” that clients talk to, and it routes requests onward.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Fill in the Blank): A request travels: Client → ________ → Server → Database.






TipAnswer Q3





The API. The API always sits between the client and the server — requests go through it on the way in, and responses come back through it on the way out.




———————


———————



Q4.
(Fill in the Blanks — the restaurant story): Fill in each blank with one word from: client, waiter, kitchen, fridge, response.

I (the _____) look at the menu and place my order with the _____. My order is carried to the _____, which pulls ingredients from the _____. The finished dish comes back to my table — that dish is the _____.







TipAnswer Q4





I (the client) look at the menu and place my order with the waiter. My order is carried to the kitchen, which pulls ingredients from the fridge. The finished dish comes back to my table — that dish is the response.
(Translation: client → API → server → database → response.)




———————


———————



Q5.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Q1): In the restaurant analogy, the API documentation is most analogous to:

The kitchen equipment
The cash register
The table number
The chef’s secret recipe book
The menu







TipAnswer Q5





e) The menu. Just like a menu tells you what’s available and how to order it, API documentation tells you what you can ask for and how to ask for it.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
text:
Part 3: Requests and Responses
Now let’s zoom in on the two key actions: requests and responses. We’ll keep this simple — the details come in Session 2.

What is a Request?
A request is the client asking for information. Here is the one thing to remember today:

A request is written as a URL — a web address.

That’s it. When we want data from an API, we build a web address that describes what we want, and we send it. In Session 2 we will dissect exactly how that web address is put together, piece by piece.
(One aside for later: some APIs also ask you to include an ID called an API key — like showing a library card. The weather API we use in this workshop is free and doesn’t need one, so we can set that idea aside for now.)


What is a Response?
The server returns a response which contains:

Data — the actual information you requested (temperature, artist name, forecast, etc.)
Metadata — information about the response (timestamps, units, etc.)
Status code — tells you whether the request was successful (e.g., 200 OK)

This information is traditionally provided in JSON format — which is exactly what Part 4 is about.






Tip🎯 Goal Check



Two halves of our goal, side by side: the request is a URL we send; the response is what we’ll format into something we can analyze.



———————



Q6.
(Fill in the Blank): A request is written as a ________ — a web address that asks the API for specific information.






TipAnswer Q6





A URL. That’s the entire request: a carefully built web address.




———————


———————



Q7.
(Multiple Choice): A response from an API contains which three things?

Data, metadata, and a status code
A URL, an API key, and a password
A plot, a table, and a summary
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Rows, columns, and cell values







TipAnswer Q7





a) A response contains the data you asked for, metadata about the response, and a status code that says whether the request worked.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
section: Part 4: Anatomy of a JSON Response
text:
Part 4: Anatomy of a JSON Response
Now let’s focus on the response — specifically, what it looks like. API responses are almost always formatted as JSON (JavaScript Object Notation).

Watch First
Step through the layers one at a time — each click reveals the next zone.



Now in Words
The animation reveals the layers of a JSON response, one at a time:

The entire thing — everything the server sends back — is called the Body (or Content). It is wrapped in curly braces { }.
Inside that body, the content is divided into three zones:

Data: what we actually wanted (temperature, city name, coordinates)
Metadata: information about the response (timestamps, units)
Status code: tells us if the request worked


Take this slowly — this structure will show up in every response for the rest of the workshop.






Tip🎯 Goal Check



The response body is the raw material. Our goal — “format the response into something we can analyze” — means taking this JSON and turning it into an R data frame.



———————



Quick Checks — JSON Response Anatomy.
(Fill in the Blanks): One or two words each.

Everything the server sends back is called the body or content, and it is wrapped in curly ________.
The three zones inside the body are the data, the ________, and the status code.
The ______ ______ tells us whether the request worked.







TipAnswers — Quick Checks






Curly braces { }
The metadata
The status code





———————



JSON Structure: Key-Value Pairs
JSON organizes data using key-value pairs. Here’s a simple example:
{
  "city": "San Luis Obispo",
  "temperature": 72,
  "units": "imperial",
  "conditions": "clear sky"
}
Key features of JSON:

Data is wrapped in curly braces { }
Each entry is a "key": value pair
Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, arrays, or nested objects
Nested objects are JSON inside JSON — like a list within a list



Nested JSON Example
{
  "city": "San Luis Obispo",
  "coordinates": {
    "lat": 35.28,
    "lon": -120.66
  },
  "weather": {
    "main": "Clear",
    "temp": 72,
    "humidity": 45
  }
}






ImportantThinking in R Terms



In R, a JSON response becomes a named list — potentially containing other named lists inside it. This is what we mean by “nested.” When we flatten it with as.data.frame(), nested keys become column names like coordinates.lat or weather.temp.



———————



Q8.
(Multiple Choice): The JSON data format, commonly used in API responses, organizes information using what fundamental structure?

Rows and columns
A nested series of bullet points
Key-value pairs
Formatted paragraphs of text
Comma-separated values







TipAnswer Q8





c) JSON data is built on key-value pairs (e.g., "city": "Chicago"), where a “key” is a string and a “value” can be a string, number, boolean, array, or another object.




———————


———————



Q9.
(Fill in the Blank): In R, a JSON object { } becomes a named ________.






TipAnswer Q9





A named list. Each JSON key becomes a name in the list, and nested JSON objects become lists inside the list.




———————


———————



Q10.
(Fill in the Blank — using the nested example above): If you flatten the nested JSON example with as.data.frame(), the column holding the latitude value would be named ________.






TipAnswer Q10





coordinates.lat — when R flattens nested JSON into a data frame, it joins the nested key names with a period. So coordinates → lat becomes coordinates.lat.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
text:
Part 5: Status Codes
Status codes tell you what happened with your request. They are grouped by category:



Range
Category
Meaning




1xx
Informational
Request received, processing…


2xx
Success
Request was successful


3xx
Redirect
Resource moved to a different URL


4xx
Client Error
Something wrong with your request


5xx
Server Error
Something wrong on the server’s end



The most important ones for data work:

200 OK — Success! You got your data.
401 Unauthorized — Your credentials (e.g., an API key) are missing or invalid.
403 Forbidden — You don’t have permission to access this resource.
404 Not Found — The endpoint or resource doesn’t exist.
429 Too Many Requests — You’ve hit the rate limit.
500 Internal Server Error — The server broke; not your fault.







NotePractical Tip



In most data API work, your goal is to get a 200 response. If you don’t, the status code tells you where to look for the problem — your request (4xx) or their server (5xx).








Tip🎯 Goal Check



The status code is the first thing we check after making a request: a 200 means “the response arrived — go ahead and format it for analysis.”



———————


Q11.
(Fill in the Blank): A status code in the 4xx range means the mistake is on the ________ side; a 5xx code means the problem is on the ________ side.






TipAnswer Q11





4xx = the client side (you — your URL or request has a problem). 5xx = the server side (them — their system broke).




———————


———————



Q12.
(Multiple Choice): Your script fails with a 404 Not Found status code. What is the most likely source of the error?

The weather company’s server crashed.
Your internet is disconnected.
R is not installed correctly.
The database deleted your account.
The URL in your request is incorrect or misspelled.







TipAnswer Q12





e) A 404 Not Found is a client-side (4xx) error — you asked for a “page” that doesn’t exist on the server. The most likely culprit is a typo or mistake in the URL you built.




———————


———————



Q13.
(Multiple Choice — Callback to Q8): If you receive a response with a status code of 200 and the body contains JSON, which of the following would you expect to find in that response?

An error message explaining what went wrong
Key-value pairs containing the data you requested
A redirect URL to a different API
An empty response with no content
A request for payment







TipAnswer Q13





b) A 200 OK status means success, and the JSON body will contain the key-value pairs with the data you requested — temperature, coordinates, city name, etc.




———————

title: Session 1: JSON Fundamentals & Request/Response
text:
Session 1 Recap
In this session, we covered the conceptual foundation for working with APIs:

What an API is — a controlled interface for software-to-software communication (the waiter!)
API data flow — Client → API → Server → Database (and back)
Requests vs. Responses — a request is a URL you send; a response is what comes back
JSON format — key-value pairs, nesting, and how it maps to R data structures
Status codes — how to diagnose what happened with your request

Up next in Session 2: We’ll learn about CRUD operations, HTTP methods (GET vs. POST), URL anatomy, and make our first requests to a dummy server!

title: Session 3: Weather API — First Real Requests & Geocoding
text:
Part 1: Meet the Open-Meteo API
We will use Open-Meteo — a free weather API built for exactly this kind of learning:

No sign-up. No API key. No credit card. You can start making requests immediately.
The main endpoint is:


request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast")

That address — https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — is the endpoint from Session 2: the stable “front door” that never changes. Everything else we want (which city, which measurements, which units) goes in the query string.






NoteWhat About API Keys, Clients & Secrets?



Many commercial APIs (OpenWeather, X, Spotify, …) require you to register and receive credentials — an API key, sometimes a client ID and secret — which you attach to every request like an ID card, and which you must store carefully (never directly in your script!). It’s an important real-world concept, and the Practice Labs on this site show it in action.
But today we get to skip all of it. Open-Meteo is free and open — so we can spend our hour on the actual skill: requests and responses.








Tip🎯 Goal Check



One endpoint, no key, live data. The only thing between us and the goal is building the query string — which you already learned to read yesterday.



———————


Q1.
(Fill in the Blank): The stable part of the URL — https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast — that never changes from one request to the next is called the ________.






TipAnswer Q1





The endpoint. The changing part (after the ?) is the query string.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Multiple Choice): Which statement about the Open-Meteo API is true?

It requires a paid subscription.
It requires an API key stored in .Renviron.
It is free and requires no API key at all.
It only works inside Positron.
It only returns data for cities in Europe.







TipAnswer Q2





c) Open-Meteo is free and open — no key, no registration. (Many other APIs do require a key; that’s the “ID card” concept from the callout above.)




———————

section: Part 2: See It in the Browser First
text:
Part 2: See It in the Browser First
Here is the payoff of Session 2’s URL anatomy: a request is just a URL — so a web browser can make one.
Copy this URL and paste it into a new browser tab, exactly as it is:
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66&current=temperature_2m&temperature_unit=fahrenheit
Try it now. What comes back is not a web page — it is raw JSON, right there in your browser:
{
  "latitude": 35.28,
  "longitude": -120.66,
  "timezone": "GMT",
  "current_units": { "time": "iso8601", "temperature_2m": "°F" },
  "current": {
    "time": "2026-08-06T16:00",
    "temperature_2m": 71.4
  }
}
Look at what you can already recognize from Sessions 1 and 2:

The endpoint and the query string in the address bar (?, &, key-value pairs)
The response wrapped in curly braces { } — the body
Data (temperature_2m: 71.4), and metadata (current_units, timezone)
Your browser made a GET request — typing a URL into the address bar is always a GET

Now change latitude=35.28&longitude=-120.66 to another location (Boston is latitude=42.36&longitude=-71.06) and reload. Live data, different city, same endpoint.






Tip🎯 Goal Check



You just completed the first half of the goal — you made a request — with zero code. R is only going to automate what the browser just did.



———————


Q3.
(Fill in the Blank): When you paste the request URL into a browser, what comes back is not a web page — it is raw ________.






TipAnswer Q3





JSON — the same body/content structure we studied in Session 1, Part 4.




———————


———————



Q4.
(Multiple Choice): Typing a URL into the browser’s address bar and pressing Enter performs which kind of HTTP request?

POST
DELETE
PUT
PATCH
GET







TipAnswer Q4





e) The address bar always makes a GET request — you are reading data, exactly like our R scripts will.




———————

section: Part 3: The ETV Cycle — Our Map for the Rest of the Workshop
text:
Part 3: The ETV Cycle — Our Map for the Rest of the Workshop

Everything we do from here on follows one repeating cycle — ETV:









Step
Name
What it means
In code




E
Extract
Make the request, receive the JSON response
request() → req_url_query() → req_perform()


T
Transform
Format the response into a data frame
resp_body_json() → tibble()


V
Visualize
Turn the data frame into a plot
ggplot()



We’ll do E and T in this session and add V in Session 4. Whenever you feel lost in code, ask: which ETV step am I on right now?

Load Libraries

library(httr2)       # E: makes web requests
library(tibble)      # T: tidyverse data frames
library(dplyr)       # T: data manipulation
library(purrr)       # T: map() — apply a recipe to many inputs
library(ggplot2)     # V: visualizations







Tip🎯 Goal Check



ETV is the goal sentence, written as three letters: E = make a request, T = format the response, V = analyze it.

title: Session 3: Weather API — First Real Requests & Geocoding
section: Part 4: Extract — The Browser Request, Now in R
text:
Part 4: Extract — The Browser Request, Now in R
Let’s have R do exactly what the browser just did. Two steps to build the request, one to send it:

# E is for Extract ------------------------------------------

# Step 1: Start from the endpoint and add the query
req <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
  req_url_query(
    latitude = 35.28,
    longitude = -120.66,
    current = "temperature_2m",
    temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
  )

# Step 2: Look at the URL R built for us — same as the browser one!
req

# Step 3: Send the request
response <- req_perform(req)

# Step 4: Check the status code
resp_status(response)

The status should be 200 — success, just like Session 1 taught us to expect.






Notereq_url_query() Writes the URL for You



Each argument becomes one key=value pair in the query string, and httr2 handles the ?, the &, and any special-character encoding automatically. Printing req shows the finished URL — compare it character-by-character with the one you pasted into your browser.



# Step 5: Parse the JSON body into a named list
result <- resp_body_json(response)

# Step 6: Peek at the structure
str(result, max.level = 2)


———————


Q5.
(Fill in the Blank): After req_perform(), we call resp_status(response) and hope to see the number ________.






TipAnswer Q5





200 — the “OK” success code. Anything in the 4xx range would mean we made a mistake in the request; 5xx would mean the server had a problem.




———————


———————



Q6.
(Multiple Choice): What does req_url_query() do?

It sends the request to the server.
It parses the JSON response.
It checks the status code.
It adds key=value pairs to the URL’s query string, handling ?, &, and encoding for you.
It draws a plot of the response.







TipAnswer Q6





d) req_url_query() builds the query string onto the endpoint. Sending is req_perform(), parsing is resp_body_json().




———————

title: Session 3: Weather API — First Real Requests & Geocoding
section: Part 5: Transform — From JSON to a Data Frame
text:
Part 5: Transform — From JSON to a Data Frame
The parsed result is a named list (Session 1!). The piece we care about is result$current:

# T is for Transform ----------------------------------------

result$current

# Pull the values we want into a tibble
current_df <- tibble(
  city   = "San Luis Obispo",
  time   = result$current$time,
  temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
)

current_df

That’s E and T — the entire workshop goal — in about ten lines.

Scaling Up: Many Cities with map()
What if we want several cities? We don’t need to copy-paste the code three times, and we don’t need to write our own function either. We give pmap() a recipe — an anonymous function, written \(...) — and it applies the recipe to every row of a small table:

# A small table of cities and their coordinates
cities <- tribble(
  ~city,             ~latitude, ~longitude,
  "San Luis Obispo",     35.28,    -120.66,
  "Boston",              42.36,     -71.06,
  "Ames",                42.03,     -93.62
)

# The recipe: for one row (one city), do E and T, return a one-row tibble
current_df <- cities |>
  pmap(\(city, latitude, longitude) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast") |>
      req_url_query(
        latitude = latitude,
        longitude = longitude,
        current = "temperature_2m",
        temperature_unit = "fahrenheit"
      ) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform
    tibble(
      city   = city,
      time   = result$current$time,
      temp_f = result$current$temperature_2m
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

current_df







NoteReading the map Pattern




\(city, latitude, longitude) { ... } is an anonymous function — a recipe with no name. The \( ) lists the ingredients; the { } holds the steps.
pmap() runs the recipe once per row of cities.
Each run returns a one-row tibble; bind_rows() stacks them into one data frame.

Same ETV steps as before — just repeated for us, without copy-paste and without defining named functions.



———————



Q7.
(Multiple Choice): In the code above, what does \(city, latitude, longitude) mean?

It creates three new columns in the tibble.
It is an anonymous function — a nameless recipe whose inputs are one row’s city, latitude, and longitude.
It deletes the variables city, latitude, and longitude.
It is a comment that R ignores.
It is a file path.







TipAnswer Q7





b) \( ) is R’s shorthand for function( ). It defines a small nameless function on the spot, which pmap() then applies to every row.




———————


———————



Q8.
(Fill in the Blank): After pmap() returns a list of one-row tibbles, we stack them into a single data frame using ________.






TipAnswer Q8





bind_rows() — it binds the rows of each small tibble into one combined tibble.




———————

title: Session 3: Weather API — First Real Requests & Geocoding
section: Part 6: Geocoding — Where Do the Coordinates Come From?
text:
Part 6: Geocoding — Where Do the Coordinates Come From?
We typed the latitude and longitude by hand. But Open-Meteo also has a geocoding endpoint that converts a city name into coordinates. Browser first, as always — paste this:
https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=San+Luis+Obispo&count=1
You’ll see JSON with a results array whose first entry contains latitude, longitude, population, and more. Now the same thing in R — with map() and an anonymous function again:

city_names <- c("San Luis Obispo", "Boston", "Ames")

coords_df <- city_names |>
  map(\(nm) {

    # E: extract
    result <- request("https://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search") |>
      req_url_query(name = nm, count = 1) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

    # T: transform (first hit in the results array)
    hit <- result$results[[1]]
    tibble(
      city      = nm,
      latitude  = round(hit$latitude, 2),
      longitude = round(hit$longitude, 2)
    )
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

coords_df

Now we can find any city’s coordinates — which Session 4 will need, because the historical weather endpoint only speaks latitude/longitude.






Tip🎯 Goal Check



Notice we just ran the same ETV pattern a third time — different endpoint, same skills. That’s the whole trick: every API interaction is the same cycle.



———————


Q9.
(Fill in the Blank): The geocoding endpoint converts a city name into ________ and ________.






TipAnswer Q9





Latitude and longitude — the coordinates the forecast and historical endpoints require.




———————

my_df





———————



Q10.
(Ordering — from Session 2): Put the following steps in the correct order for making an API request in R. Write the letters in order.

Parse the JSON response into a data frame
Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
Check the status code for success (200)
Send the request using req_perform()
Create a request object with request()







TipAnswer Q10





b → e → d → c → a

b) Construct the URL with endpoint and query parameters
e) Create a request object with request()
d) Send the request using req_perform()
c) Check the status code for success (200)
a) Parse the JSON response into a data frame

(In practice, request() + req_url_query() do steps b and e together.)

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
text:
The Cat API is deliberately low-stakes — but it teaches something important. Unlike NASA (key in the URL), this API expects your credential in an HTTP request header (x-api-key). That one change in technique is the key learning of this lab.

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
text:
Step 1 — Get Your API Key

Go to thecatapi.com and click Get Your API Key
Enter your email — the key arrives instantly
Add it to your .Renviron file:

CAT_KEY=your_key_here






NoteNo Key? No Problem — For Now



The Cat API works without a key for basic endpoints, returning a small subset of data. This is intentional — you’ll use the unauthenticated version first in Exercise 1 to see the contrast.

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
text:
Step 2 — Setup

library(httr2)
library(dplyr)
library(glue)
library(dotenv)

load_dot_env()
cat_key <- Sys.getenv("CAT_KEY")

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
section: Exercise 1: Authenticated vs. Unauthenticated — See the Difference
text:
Exercise 1: Authenticated vs. Unauthenticated — See the Difference
This exercise makes the value of authentication concrete by running the same request both ways.

Without a key (unauthenticated)

req_no_auth <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/images/search")
response_no_auth <- req_perform(req_no_auth)

result_no_auth <- resp_body_json(response_no_auth)

cat("Fields returned (no auth):", paste(names(result_no_auth[[1]]), collapse=", "), "\n")
cat("Number of results:", length(result_no_auth), "\n")



With a key (authenticated)
Notice the only change is the addition of req_headers().

req_auth <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/images/search") |>
  req_headers("x-api-key" = cat_key)

response_auth <- req_perform(req_auth)
result_auth   <- resp_body_json(response_auth)

cat("Fields returned (with auth):", paste(names(result_auth[[1]]), collapse=", "), "\n")







ImportantWhat changed?



Look at the field lists side by side. Authenticated responses include breeds, categories, and breed_ids — fields that are gated behind auth. This is a common API design pattern: basic access is free, richer data requires a credential.

section: Exercise 2: Search for Images with Limit & Size
text:
Exercise 2: Search for Images with Limit & Size

req <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/images/search") |>
  req_headers("x-api-key" = cat_key) |>
  req_url_query(limit = 10, size = "med")

response <- req_perform(req)
images   <- resp_body_json(response)

cat("Number of images returned:", length(images), "\n")

# Extract URLs
urls <- sapply(images, function(img) img$url)
print(urls)

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
text:
Exercise 3: Retrieve Breed Information
The Cat API has a /breeds endpoint that returns a list of all cat breeds with detailed attributes.

req <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/breeds") |>
  req_headers("x-api-key" = cat_key)

response <- req_perform(req)
breeds   <- resp_body_json(response)

cat("Total breeds available:", length(breeds), "\n")
cat("Fields per breed:", paste(names(breeds[[1]]), collapse=", "), "\n")


# Flatten into a data frame
breed_df <- lapply(breeds, function(b) {
  data.frame(
    name              = b$name,
    origin            = b$origin %||% NA_character_,
    life_span         = b$life_span %||% NA_character_,
    temperament       = b$temperament %||% NA_character_,
    intelligence      = b$intelligence %||% NA_integer_,
    affection_level   = b$affection_level %||% NA_integer_,
    energy_level      = b$energy_level %||% NA_integer_,
    stringsAsFactors  = FALSE
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

glimpse(breed_df)


# What are the most intelligent breeds?
breed_df |>
  arrange(desc(intelligence)) |>
  select(name, origin, intelligence, energy_level, affection_level) |>
  head(10)

section: Exercise 4: Search for Images of a Specific Breed
text:
Exercise 4: Search for Images of a Specific Breed
Combine what you’ve learned — use a breed ID from Exercise 3 to search for images of that specific breed.

# Get the breed ID for Abyssinian
abyssinian_id <- breed_df |>
  filter(name == "Abyssinian") |>
  pull(name)

# Use the breeds endpoint to find the actual ID
abyssinian_entry <- breeds[[which(sapply(breeds, function(b) b$name) == "Abyssinian")]]
breed_id <- abyssinian_entry$id

cat("Breed ID:", breed_id, "\n")

# Search for images of that breed
req <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/images/search") |>
  req_headers("x-api-key" = cat_key) |>
  req_url_query(breed_ids = breed_id, limit = 5)

breed_images <- resp_body_json(req_perform(req))
cat("Images found:", length(breed_images), "\n")
sapply(breed_images, function(img) img$url)

title: Practice Lab 2: The Cat API
text:
Questions

———————


Q1.
(Conceptual): In Exercise 1, you ran the same endpoint twice — once without a key and once with one. The URL was identical both times. Where exactly did the credential travel in the authenticated request?






TipAnswer Q1





The credential traveled in the HTTP request header — specifically the x-api-key header. It is not part of the URL, query string, or response body. Headers are transmitted in the request metadata, which is separate from the URL and typically not logged in the same places a URL would be.




———————


———————



Q2.
(Code — Callback to Lab 1): In Lab 1 (NASA), the API key was passed as ?api_key=KEY in the URL. Rewrite the unauthenticated Cat API request from Exercise 1 as if the Cat API used a query parameter instead of a header. What would that look like using req_url_query()?






TipAnswer Q2





req_param_style <- request("https://api.thecatapi.com/v1/images/search") |>
  req_url_query(api_key = cat_key)
This is a hypothetical — the Cat API doesn’t actually support this. But the exercise shows that req_url_query() and req_headers() are the two different tools for two different auth patterns, and that the API documentation tells you which one to use.




———————


———————



Q3.
(Analysis): Using breed_df, which origin country has the highest average intelligence score across all its breeds? Use dplyr to find out.






TipAnswer Q3





breed_df |>
  filter(!is.na(intelligence), !is.na(origin)) |>
  group_by(origin) |>
  summarise(avg_intelligence = mean(intelligence, na.rm = TRUE), count = n()) |>
  arrange(desc(avg_intelligence)) |>
  head(5)
Countries with only one or two breeds may score high just by chance — look at the count column alongside the average.

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
Lab 1 — NASA Open APIs

Learning Objectives

Retrieve data from a real scientific API
Practice GET requests with API key as a query parameter
Work with deeply nested JSON (NEO asteroid data)



Setup Time
~5 minutes. Students sign up at api.nasa.gov — the key arrives by email immediately. Alternatively, DEMO_KEY works out of the box (30 requests/hour limit).


Key Teaching Points

The API key goes in the URL as a query parameter (?api_key=...)
APOD returns a single JSON object; NEO returns a multi-level nested structure
The NEO response requires iteration (lapply) to flatten before analysis



Common Errors








Error
Likely Cause
Fix




403 Forbidden
DEMO_KEY rate limit hit
Wait 1 hour, or register for a free personal key


400 Bad Request on NEO
Date range exceeds 7 days
Shorten the range to ≤ 7 days


Empty $url in APOD
Media type is video, not image
Check apod$media_type first





Discussion Prompt

“The key is in the URL. What happens to security when you share that URL with someone else?”

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
Lab 2 — The Cat API

Learning Objectives

Pass credentials in an HTTP header instead of the URL
Understand why header-based auth is more secure
Practice req_headers() in httr2



Setup Time
~3 minutes. Free API key at thecatapi.com. The API works without a key for basic endpoints, which is useful for demonstrating the difference between authenticated and unauthenticated requests in class.


Key Teaching Points

The x-api-key header is a custom header — not all APIs use the same header name
Header contents are not visible in the URL or browser history
Unauthenticated requests return a smaller subset of results — a good live demo



Common Errors








Error
Likely Cause
Fix




Empty results on /votes
These endpoints require auth
Confirm the header is being set


401 on favorite endpoints
Key not passed or malformed
Print req object before performing to inspect headers





Discussion Prompt

“Why would an API designer choose headers over query parameters for credentials? What does the URL look like in each case?”



Classroom Demo
Run the breed search request twice — once with the header and once without. Show students the difference in the response payload (authenticated responses include breed_temperament and other premium fields).

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
Lab 3 — OpenWeather (Extended)

Learning Objectives

Apply skills from Sessions 3–4 to new endpoints (Air Quality, Forecast)
Compare data across multiple cities using iteration
Explore multi-call workflows



Setup Time
~10 minutes. The core workshop now uses the keyless Open-Meteo API, so students will not already have an OpenWeather key — they sign up at openweathermap.org (key activation can take up to 2 hours, so assign signup as pre-work).


Key Teaching Points

The Air Quality Index endpoint requires coordinates (lat/lon), not a city name — reinforcing geocoding from Session 3
The 5-day forecast response nests list (an array of 40 time-step objects) — good practice at .[[1]] indexing
Comparing cities with lapply introduces the pattern of writing a function once and mapping it



Common Errors








Error
Likely Cause
Fix




401 on all calls
Key not yet activated (takes up to 2 hours after signup)
Use a pre-made key for class; students activate theirs at home


Empty list in forecast
Wrong response path — use $list not $forecast
names(resp_body_json(response)) to inspect top-level keys





Discussion Prompt

“The forecast endpoint returns 40 time steps (3-hour intervals over 5 days). What would a tidy data frame of this look like, and how would you get there?”

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
Lab 4 — TMDB Movie Database

Learning Objectives

Authenticate with both an API key and a Bearer token
Understand the difference between the two approaches
Recognize the Authorization: Bearer ... pattern used in professional APIs



Setup Time
~8 minutes. Students register at themoviedb.org, go to Settings → API, and receive both an API Key (v3) and a Read Access Token (v4 Bearer). Both are on the same settings page.


Key Teaching Points

The API Key goes in the URL (?api_key=...) — same pattern as NASA
The Bearer token goes in the Authorization header (Authorization: Bearer TOKEN)
Bearer tokens are the industry standard in modern APIs (OAuth 2.0 pattern)
TMDB’s /search/movie endpoint introduces pagination via ?page=



Common Errors








Error
Likely Cause
Fix




401 with Bearer token
Token copied with extra whitespace
Re-copy and check nchar(token)


Empty results array
Search query URL-encoded incorrectly
Use req_url_query(query = "movie name") instead of manual encoding


404 on endpoint
Wrong API version — v3 vs v4
Confirm endpoint starts with /3/ for v3 key auth





Discussion Prompt

“You’ve now used three auth methods: query param (NASA, TMDB key), custom header (Cat API x-api-key), and Authorization Bearer (TMDB token). As a developer choosing how to secure an API, what would drive that decision?”

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
Lab 5 — GitHub REST API

Learning Objectives

Make unauthenticated requests to a public API
Create and use a Personal Access Token (PAT) with scoped permissions
Understand the principle of least-privilege in API authorization



Setup Time

Unauthenticated exercises: zero setup
PAT creation: ~5 minutes at github.com → Settings → Developer Settings → Fine-grained tokens



Key Teaching Points

GitHub’s public endpoints work without any authentication — good entry point
Rate limits differ significantly: 60 req/hour unauthenticated vs. 5,000 req/hour with a token
Fine-grained tokens let students explicitly choose what permissions to grant — a live demonstration of least-privilege security
The User-Agent header is required by GitHub’s API



Common Errors








Error
Likely Cause
Fix




403 or requires authentication
Endpoint requires auth (e.g., private repos)
Switch to PAT-authenticated request


422 Unprocessable Entity on search
Query syntax error
Check GitHub search syntax — strings must be URL-encoded


401 with PAT
Token expired or wrong scope
Check token expiry date and permissions in GitHub settings





Discussion Prompt

“You created a fine-grained token that can only read public repositories. If that token were accidentally leaked in a public repo, what damage could an attacker do with it? What if it had ‘write’ permissions?”



Classroom Demo
Search for repositories with the topic "tidyverse" using the GitHub search API. Shows students how to discover open-source projects programmatically — a direct real-world use case.

title: Instructor Guide — Practice Labs
text:
General Troubleshooting

Diagnosing Any API Error
Teach students this four-step debugging process:
# Step 1: Check the status code
resp_status(response)

# Step 2: Read the error message body
resp_body_string(response)

# Step 3: Inspect the request that was sent
req  # print the request object to see URL, headers

# Step 4: Check the API documentation for that status code


Rate Limits
All free-tier APIs in these labs have rate limits. If a class of 30 students all hit an API simultaneously, shared IP limits can trigger 429 Too Many Requests. Strategies:

Use staggered start times (group 1 starts on NASA, group 2 starts on Cat API)
Each student should use their own API key, not a shared one
Add Sys.sleep(1) between repeated calls in loop exercises



.Renviron Pattern (Remind Students)
All labs expect keys to be stored in .Renviron and loaded with dotenv::load_dot_env() or readRenviron("~/.Renviron").
# In .Renviron (never commit this file):
NASA_KEY=your_nasa_key_here
CAT_KEY=your_cat_api_key_here
TMDB_KEY=your_tmdb_api_key_here
TMDB_TOKEN=your_tmdb_bearer_token_here
GITHUB_TOKEN=your_github_pat_here

# In R:
dotenv::load_dot_env()
nasa_key <- Sys.getenv("NASA_KEY")

title: Practice Lab 3: OpenWeather Extended
text:
Exercise 1: Air Quality Index
The AQI endpoint requires latitude and longitude, not a city name. This means you need to geocode first — exactly the pattern from Session 3.

Step 1a — Geocode a city

get_coordinates <- function(city, key) {
  url <- glue("http://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?q={city}&limit=1&appid={key}")
  result <- resp_body_json(req_perform(request(url)))
  list(lat = result[[1]]$lat, lon = result[[1]]$lon)
}

coords <- get_coordinates("San Luis Obispo", weather_key)
cat("Lat:", coords$lat, "| Lon:", coords$lon, "\n")



Step 1b — Fetch air quality

aqi_url <- glue(
  "http://api.openweathermap.org/data/2.5/air_pollution",
  "?lat={coords$lat}&lon={coords$lon}&appid={weather_key}"
)

response <- req_perform(request(aqi_url))
aqi_data <- resp_body_json(response)

# AQI scale: 1=Good, 2=Fair, 3=Moderate, 4=Poor, 5=Very Poor
aqi_value  <- aqi_data$list[[1]]$main$aqi
components <- aqi_data$list[[1]]$components

cat("Air Quality Index:", aqi_value, "\n")
cat("PM2.5:", components$pm2_5, "μg/m³\n")
cat("CO:",    components$co,    "μg/m³\n")
cat("NO2:",   components$no2,   "μg/m³\n")
cat("O3:",    components$o3,    "μg/m³\n")
